{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "The lighthouse at Corran Point had been automated the year Ellis turned sixty, and the Board had sent a man in a gray coat to explain the sensors and thank him for his service. Ellis had listened, nodded, and kept the cottage, because the lease ran another decade and no one had thought to ask him to leave.

His granddaughter Tove came out in the summers, then stayed one autumn and did not go back. She was twenty and mended nets for the harbor boats and read the tide tables the way other people read the news.

Ellis had not taught her the lamp. The lamp ran itself now. He had taught her the sea. How the swell arrived from a storm still two hundred miles out, long and slow, before any cloud showed. How the gulls went quiet and sat facing inland when the glass was falling. How the foghorn's echo came back wrong off the headland when the fog was thickening faster than the sensors could tell.

In November the automated horn failed. A relay corroded, and the fault light blinked in an office forty miles away where no one was on duty after six.

Tove heard the silence first. She stood at the window and watched the fog swallow the point, and out past the skerries she saw the running lights of the evening ferry, low and steady, coming in on the wrong bearing.

She took the hand bell from the shelf and the old brass horn her grandfather had kept polished for no reason he would admit. She climbed the gallery stairs and sounded it, three long, one short, the way he had shown her once, until the ferry's lights swung wide and slid safely into the channel.

By morning the Board sent a man to ask who had sounded a horn that no longer existed.

Tove said only that someone still watched the point."}
